name: Siddha medicine

card.summary: A traditional Tamil system of herbal, mineral, diet, yoga and massage care that practitioners apply to skin, hair and general vitality, and so to how a person looks.
card.aka: Siddha system, Tamil traditional medicine, Siddha vaidyam
card.note: Some traditional preparations contain processed mercury or other metals; case reports of mercury poisoning from traditional Indian medicines exist.

quick.overview:
Siddha medicine is a traditional healing system from Tamil Nadu in southern India. It treats health as a balance of three forces (vaadham, pittham, kapam) and uses herbs, processed minerals, diet rules, yoga, massage and pressure-point work.

For appearance, practitioners use it for skin conditions such as psoriasis, eczema, vitiligo and hair loss, and for rejuvenation. The idea is that clearer skin, healthier hair and better vitality show up in how a person looks. Published work is mostly reviews and small studies.
quick.how: People consult a registered Siddha practitioner, who assesses the person using traditional diagnostic methods and prescribes herbal or herbo-mineral preparations, external oils or pastes, and diet and lifestyle rules. Treatments are typically taken over weeks to months. Practitioners are trained in a state-recognised degree course in India.
quick.risks: Some herbo-mineral preparations use mercury, sulfur and arsenic that are processed before use. Case reports describe kidney damage from mercury in traditional Indian medicines, and the quality of purification varies. Indian regulators license practitioners, but the Indian Medical Association has criticised the system. People with medical conditions are generally advised by clinicians to tell their doctor about any traditional product they use.

lead: Siddha medicine is a traditional medical system of the Tamil people of southern India, regarded by its practitioners as one of the oldest in the country [1][2]. Its teachings are attributed to the Siddhars, sages said to have gained supernatural knowledge, with Agastya (Agasthyar) regarded as the founding figure [1][3]. The system uses herbal, animal and inorganic preparations, dietary and lifestyle rules, yoga and external therapies [1][3].

For appearance, Siddha is used mainly through its treatment of skin and hair problems and through rejuvenation practices (kayakalpa). A clinical dermatology review describes Siddha herbal and herbo-mineral treatments for psoriasis, eczema, alopecia, warts, vitiligo and other skin diseases, with diet and lifestyle changes as part of care [2]. Proponents' goal is clearer skin, restored hair and a healthier, younger look [2][3].

Research on Siddha is mostly narrative reviews, laboratory and in-silico work and small trials, several of them on COVID-19 decoctions rather than on skin or appearance [4][5][6]. Heavy-metal content in some traditional medicines has been documented in case reports of mercury poisoning [7]. In India the system is regulated under the Ministry of AYUSH, with a formal degree course [1][3].

chain: Herbal or herbo-mineral internal and external treatment plus diet rules
Targeted skin or hair condition and general vitality
Clearer skin, healthier hair, a more rejuvenated look
angle.text: Practitioners apply Siddha treatments to skin diseases, hair loss and general rejuvenation, so that the skin and hair people see in the mirror improve. The results people report depend on the condition treated and the preparation used.

paras: Siddha teaches that five elements (earth, water, fire, air and sky) are present in the body, in food and in medicines [1]. Health is described as a balance of three forces, called mukkuttram: vaadham (airy), pittham (fiery) and kapam (watery), and illness as a disturbance of that balance by diet, climate, activity or stress [1][2].

Diagnosis uses a set of eight traditional methods of examination that are used to determine diagnosis, cause and outlook [2]. Remedies fall into three groups: plant products, animal products and inorganic substances, the last including preparations built on sulfur and mercury [1]. Diet and lifestyle rules (pathiyam and apathiyam) accompany treatment [1]. Practitioners also use yoga, meditation, massage and varmam, a pressure-point therapy [4].

Traditional accounts trace Siddha to Shiva, who is said to have taught Parvati, with the sage Agastya and eighteen Siddhars as its main authorities [1]. The Siddhars wrote in Tamil on medicine, yoga and astrology [2]. Knowledge was traditionally passed from teacher to student, and the Siddhars later became local healers [1].

A 2023 historical study examines the rise of Siddha as a named medical system in the Madras Presidency in the 1920s and 1930s, when Tamil-speaking practitioners organised their tradition as a distinct system [8]. In the modern state, a central council set up in 1971 oversees education in Indian systems of medicine, and a degree course of about five and a half years is offered in Tamil Nadu [1].

sections.h: Use for skin, hair and rejuvenation
paras: A 2008 review in Clinics in Dermatology by a Siddha practitioner describes treatments for psoriasis, eczema, alopecia, diabetic ulcers, warts, vitiligo, pemphigus, leprosy and other skin diseases, delivered as herbal and herbo-mineral preparations alongside dietary changes [2]. Hair loss and skin pigment disorders are among the appearance-related conditions named [2].

Rejuvenation (kayakalpa) is a further branch, described in Grokipedia's summary as a use of the system aimed at longevity and renewed vitality [3]. Practitioners present these treatments as improving the whole person, including skin quality and the look of health.

No randomized trial of Siddha treatment specifically for cosmetic skin or hair outcomes has been published. The dermatology review is a practitioner's overview of principles and uses, not a trial [2].

Human trials of Siddha products have focused on other conditions. Randomized trials in India tested the Siddha decoctions Kabasura Kudineer and Nilavembu Kudineer in COVID-19; one open-label trial reported lower viral load with Kabasura Kudineer than with vitamin C and zinc [5], and a double-blind placebo-controlled trial tested two decoctions together with standard care [6]. A 2025 review discusses Siddha herbs and non-invasive therapies in neurological disorders and calls for integration with modern neuroscience [4]. Laboratory and animal studies cover plants used in Siddha for diabetes and for infections [9][10].
Reviews of safety flag a separate issue: a case series reported chronic mercury poisoning with kidney damage (membranous nephropathy) in patients taking traditional Indian medicines [7].

Siddha mineral preparations are processed by purification and calcination methods that practitioners say reduce toxicity [3]. Researchers and clinicians have raised concern about metal content when processing is inadequate, and case reports link some traditional medicines to mercury poisoning [7].

In India, graduates register and prescribe under the Siddha Pharmacopoeia within the Drugs and Cosmetics Act of 1940 [1]. A 2018 Supreme Court of India judgment warned of risks from unqualified practitioners, and the Indian Medical Association has criticised Siddha degrees and therapies since 2014 [1].

timeline.event: Siddha is organised as a distinct medical system in the Madras Presidency [8].
Central Council of Indian Medicine established to oversee education in Indian systems of medicine [1].
Clinics in Dermatology review describes Siddha treatments for skin diseases [2].
Supreme Court of India judgment warns of risks from unqualified traditional practitioners [1].
Randomized trials of Siddha decoctions in COVID-19 are published [5][6].
